tiles.label: CT Safe Connect / CCADV — 24/7
tiles.say: CT Safe Connect is the statewide hotline run by the Connecticut Coalition Against Domestic Violence. Call or text 1-888-774-2900. Free, confidential, twenty-four hours, in English. For Spanish, 1-844-831-9200. They connect you to all eighteen CCADV member shelter programs and help with bed-finding, safety planning, transportation, and crisis counseling. If you are leaving an abusive partner, family member, or housemate, this is the right first call. Deaf or hard-of-hearing callers can use 7-1-1 relay or VRS.

tiles.label: Interval House — 24/7
tiles.say: Interval House — one of the largest DV shelters in CT, serving Greater Hartford. Twenty-four hour hotline 860-838-8467. They also have community-based services if you do not need shelter.

tiles.label: SANE exam tonight
tiles.say: For a Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner exam tonight: call the Connecticut Alliance to End Sexual Violence — formerly CONNSACS — at 1-888-999-5545 in English or 1-888-568-8332 in Spanish. They will route you to the nearest CT SANE-program hospital and send an advocate to be with you. The exam is free, regardless of whether you choose to report to police. To preserve evidence: do not shower, do not change clothes, do not douche, and if possible avoid using the bathroom before the exam.

tiles.label: National DV Hotline — 24/7
tiles.say: National Domestic Violence Hotline. 1-800-799-7233. For Deaf callers, video-phone 1-855-812-1001 or use 7-1-1 relay. Text START to 88788. Free, confidential, twenty-four hours. Useful if you are relocating out of Connecticut or want a second option alongside the CT statewide line.

tiles.label: Human Trafficking — 24/7
tiles.say: National Human Trafficking Hotline. 1-888-373-7888 or text HELP to 233733. They can connect trafficking survivors with anti-trafficking advocates in Connecticut who help plan a safer exit and look for safe housing options. Twenty-four hours, confidential.

tiles.label: No shelter bed tonight?
tiles.say: If shelter beds are full in your area, the CT Safe Connect hotline can help look for other options — including possible emergency hotel placement through partner agencies. Availability is never guaranteed, but ask directly: "are there any other safe-housing options for tonight?"

tiles.label: Safety planning conversation
tiles.say: A safety plan is a personalized step-by-step for getting yourself (and children, pets) out safely. CCADV and NDVH hotline staff are trained to walk you through one — what to pack, where to go first, what to leave behind, what to tell whom. This is free and takes thirty to sixty minutes.

tiles.label: Stay with someone you trust
tiles.say: If you have a friend or family member you trust to stay with, that is a valid option — but tell the CCADV hotline so they can help with the safety plan. The abuser may know about that person; CCADV will help you think it through.

tiles.label: CT survivor-protection paths
tiles.say: Connecticut law gives survivors several distinct protections. There are three different court orders — a Civil Restraining Order, a Civil Protection Order, and a Criminal Protective Order — plus the Address Confidentiality Program, which is not a court order but hides your address on public records. Each one is for a different situation. The kiosk will help you find the right path.

tiles.label: Civil restraining order
tiles.say: A Civil Restraining Order — Form JD-FM-137 — is filed in Family Court, the Superior Court Family Division. Eligibility: the person you fear is a family or household member — spouse, ex-spouse, parent, child, sibling, current or former dating partner, or housemate. Free to file. The court may grant an Ex Parte temporary order the same day; a full hearing follows within fourteen days.

tiles.label: Civil protection order
tiles.say: A Civil Protection Order is for stalking, sexual assault, or repeated patterns of harassment where the person you fear is NOT a family or household member — for example, a coworker, classmate, neighbor, or stranger. Filed in Superior Court, civil division. Free. The court evaluates the application; a hearing follows. Connecticut Legal Services and the Judicial Branch self-help center can walk you through the paperwork.

tiles.label: Criminal protective order
tiles.say: When criminal charges are filed against the person who harmed you — for example, after an arrest for assault, threatening, or stalking — a judge may issue a Criminal Protective Order as part of that case. The prosecutor handles it; you do not file it yourself. Conditions can include no contact and stay-away orders. Talk to the Office of the Victim Advocate or your case prosecutor about your rights and how to be heard.
tiles.detail: May be issued in a criminal case

tiles.label: Address Confidentiality Program (ACP)
tiles.say: The Connecticut Address Confidentiality Program — ACP — gives survivors a substitute mailing address to use on public records, so the abuser cannot find them through DMV, voter rolls, court filings, or other records. ACP is not a court order; it is a separate program administered by the CT Secretary of the State. Application requires working with an enrolling agency — most CCADV member shelters are enrolling agencies. Call 1-888-774-2900 for help getting started.
tiles.detail: Hide your address — not a court order

tiles.label: Other safety tools — by situation
tiles.say: If your situation does not match the three court orders or ACP cleanly: if guns are present in the home, ask police about a Connecticut Risk Protection Order — sometimes called a risk warrant — which is officer or family-initiated. If this is stalking or assault by someone who is not an intimate partner, ask legal aid about the Civil Protection Order path. If the contact is online — texts, social media, or platforms — save screenshots first and ask legal aid what to document. CT Legal Services at 1-800-453-3320 can help you figure out the right path for your facts.

tiles.label: OVS — Victim Compensation
tiles.say: Connecticut Office of Victim Services — OVS — provides financial compensation for crime victims for medical bills, counseling, lost wages, funeral costs, relocation expenses, and more. Apply within two years of the crime (longer for some categories). Application is free. Search "CT Office of Victim Services" or call the OVS hotline.

tiles.label: VAWA self-petition
tiles.say: The Violence Against Women Act — VAWA — allows certain abused immigrant spouses, children, and parents of US citizens or lawful permanent residents to self-petition for status, independent of the abusive family member. Eligibility is not limited by gender — cisgender men and trans people may also qualify. Connecticut immigration legal services such as IRIS in New Haven, CIRI (the Connecticut Institute for Refugees and Immigrants) in Bridgeport, and the Yale and UConn law school immigration clinics can help with VAWA petitions at no cost.

tiles.label: U-visa for crime victims
tiles.say: The U-visa provides temporary lawful status for certain crime victims — including domestic violence, sexual assault, and trafficking victims — who help law enforcement. You will need a law enforcement certification, usually signed by the investigating detective or prosecutor. CT-based free immigration legal services such as IRIS, CIRI, and the Yale and UConn law school immigration clinics can help with U-visa petitions.

tiles.label: CT Legal Services
tiles.say: Connecticut Legal Services and Statewide Legal Services. Free legal help for low-income survivors on housing, family law, public benefits. 1-800-453-3320.

tiles.label: CT VINE — release notification
tiles.say: CT VINE — Victim Information and Notification Everyday — sends an automated alert when the person in custody is released, transferred, or has a court hearing. Register online at vinelink.com (look for Connecticut), or ask the CT Department of Correction Victim Services Office for the current registration phone number. Free and confidential.

tiles.label: CT 211 — call right now
tiles.say: Dial 2-1-1 in Connecticut. Free, twenty-four hours. CT 211 is the central referral hub — food, housing, utility help, child care, transportation, mental-health services. They know what is available in your specific town this week.

tiles.label: Food pantry — local
tiles.say: For local food pantries, dial 211 and press 1 for food. They will route you to the nearest pantry by your town. Most pantries are open weekly and free — no income proof needed at most.

tiles.label: OVS emergency funds
tiles.say: CT Office of Victim Services has emergency funds for crime victims for immediate needs — relocation, security deposit, medical co-pays, mental-health services. Apply through OVS directly or through a CCADV member shelter / sexual-assault crisis center, which can submit on your behalf.

tiles.label: SNAP (food stamps)
tiles.say: SNAP — Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — covers groceries. Apply through CT Department of Social Services at ct.gov/dss or at any DSS office. If you are fleeing abuse, you can apply even if you are still legally part of the abuser household — talk to a DSS worker about emergency expedited processing.

tiles.label: TFA / cash assistance
tiles.say: Temporary Family Assistance — TFA — provides monthly cash assistance for low-income families with children. Apply through CT DSS. Survivors fleeing abuse can often get expedited processing.

tiles.label: SSDI — disability income
tiles.say: Social Security Disability Insurance — SSDI — is monthly federal income for people who can no longer work due to a long-term medical condition AND have enough recent work history. Apply at ssa.gov or any CT Social Security office. Survivors with PTSD, traumatic brain injury, severe depression, anxiety, or physical injuries from abuse may qualify. Many people are denied the first time and need to appeal — CT Legal Services or a NOSSCR-affiliated disability representative may be able to help, often for free or on contingency.

tiles.label: SSI — needs-based income
tiles.say: Supplemental Security Income — SSI — is monthly federal income for people with a disability OR age 65+, with very low income AND very few assets. No work history required. Children with disabilities may also qualify. Apply through SSA at ssa.gov or any CT office. Children who get SSI may also qualify for HUSKY, but in Connecticut you may need a separate Medicaid or HUSKY application through DSS or Access Health CT. CT Legal Services helps with applications and appeals.

tiles.label: Medicare — health coverage
tiles.say: Medicare is federal health coverage. Most people qualify at age 65. If you are entitled to SSDI, Medicare usually starts after 24 months of SSDI benefit entitlement, which is not always 24 months after your approval date — retroactive approvals can change the clock. Earlier eligibility for end-stage renal disease or ALS. Four parts: A hospital, B doctor, C Advantage plans, D drugs. The Center for Medicare Advocacy in Connecticut helps with denials. CHOICES — Connecticut’s SHIP program — through Aging and Disability Services and the Area Agencies on Aging, gives free, unbiased Medicare help to people with Medicare and their families or caregivers.

tiles.label: Utility shut-off help
tiles.say: Connecticut Energy Assistance Program — CEAP — helps low-income households with heating costs. Connecticut also has a winter shut-off protection that prevents utility disconnection November to May for eligible households. 211 routes you to the application path.

tiles.label: Clothing + basic supplies
tiles.say: For clothing, hygiene supplies, baby supplies, school supplies — most CCADV member shelters maintain donation rooms even if you are not staying overnight. Some Goodwill / Salvation Army / community closets also have free vouchers for survivors. 211 has the local listing.

tiles.label: Locksmith / security cost
tiles.say: If you need to change locks, add security cameras, or otherwise make your home safer because the abuser had access, OVS emergency funds can sometimes cover these costs. Save receipts and apply.

tiles.label: Child in immediate danger
tiles.say: If a child is in immediate physical danger, call 911 first. To report ongoing child abuse or neglect to the state, also call the Connecticut DCF Careline at 1-800-842-2288, twenty-four hours. DCF accepts reports from anyone, not only mandated reporters.

tiles.label: Bringing kids to shelter
tiles.say: Most CCADV member DV shelters accept children — bedrooms accommodate parent-plus-children, and many have on-site childcare during the day. Call 1-888-774-2900 to confirm bed availability for you AND your kids.

tiles.label: Tell school about safety changes
tiles.say: Notify your child's school of the situation — who is authorized to pick up your child, any custody changes, the school's response if the abuser comes to the building. Many CT schools have established DV / custody protocols. Bring any court orders.

tiles.label: Emergency custody / parenting orders
tiles.say: For emergency custody or emergency parenting plan changes, you can file an Ex Parte motion in Family Court the same day. Family Court counselors (often called Family Relations) help walk you through the forms. CT Legal Services at 1-800-453-3320 can also help low-income survivors.

tiles.label: Childcare while you stabilize
tiles.say: Connecticut Care 4 Kids subsidizes childcare for low-income working parents, parents in job training, and parents fleeing DV. Apply at ct.gov/oec. Some shelters have on-site childcare; CT Care 4 Kids can sometimes start immediately for DV survivors.

tiles.label: Therapy for children
tiles.say: For child mental-health support after witnessing or experiencing abuse: CCADV member shelters often have child therapists on staff or partnerships with trauma-informed providers. CT 211 also lists child-trauma therapists by region. Some specifically use evidence-based modalities like Trauma-Focused CBT.

tiles.label: Kept from my children
tiles.say: If the other parent is keeping you from your children in a way that goes against a custody order or court agreement, do not try to handle it alone. Document everything — dates, times, what was said, who saw it. Contact your family law attorney, or if you do not have one, CT Legal Services at 1-800-453-3320. If the situation is acute and you believe your child is at risk, call 911.
tiles.detail: Other parent will not return them

tiles.label: Birth certificates + IDs
tiles.say: If you fled without your children's birth certificates or IDs, you can enroll children in CT public school WITHOUT them — under McKinney-Vento (federal homeless law) and CT-specific protections, schools must enroll children of families in transition. Tell the school registrar "we are in transition."

tiles.label: SANE exam — find nearest
tiles.say: SANE — Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner — is a specialized forensic exam, free, regardless of whether you choose to report to police. To find the SANE-program hospital nearest you and get advocate support during the exam, call the Connecticut Alliance to End Sexual Violence at 1-888-999-5545 in English or 1-888-568-8332 in Spanish. Yale-New Haven Hospital operates a SANE program; many other CT hospitals do as well — the Alliance hotline knows which sites are currently active. To preserve evidence: do not shower, do not change clothes, do not douche, and if possible avoid using the bathroom before the exam.

tiles.label: Strangled / choked — go to ER
tiles.say: If someone put pressure on your neck — or you had trouble breathing, speaking, or swallowing, you passed out, or your vision went dark — please go to an emergency room now, even if you feel okay. Strangulation can cause delayed internal injuries that do not show right away: airway swelling, voice changes, swallowing problems, breathing difficulties, brain injury, and stroke risk. Many emergency rooms and SANE programs have specific strangulation evaluation protocols — ask for one.
tiles.detail: Even if you feel okay now

tiles.label: Urgent / emergency care
tiles.say: For acute injuries — go to the emergency room. For less acute injuries that still need same-day care — urgent care clinics. CT also has Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) like Charter Oak Health Center that provide free or sliding-scale care regardless of insurance status.

tiles.label: Plan B — within 72 hours
tiles.say: Plan B is an emergency-contraception pill, sold over the counter without a prescription at any pharmacy. It is most effective within seventy-two hours after unprotected sex, including sexual assault. SANE exams often offer it during the visit. Planned Parenthood at 1-800-230-7526 also provides it free or on a sliding scale.

tiles.label: ella — within 120 hours
tiles.say: ella is a different emergency-contraception medication that is effective up to one hundred twenty hours — five days — after unprotected sex. It requires a prescription. A clinician at the SANE program, Planned Parenthood at 1-800-230-7526, or an urgent care clinic can prescribe it. Some pharmacies stock it; others may need to order it.

tiles.label: STI testing + PEP
tiles.say: After sexual assault, STI testing and post-exposure prophylaxis — PEP for HIV — should happen within seventy-two hours for PEP effectiveness. SANE programs handle this. Without a SANE exam, urgent care or Planned Parenthood can also provide PEP and STI testing.

tiles.label: DV-aware counseling
tiles.say: CCADV member shelters all provide free counseling for survivors — both individual therapy and support groups. The counselors are trauma-informed and DV-specialized. You do not need to be staying at a shelter to use the counseling. Call 1-888-774-2900.

tiles.label: Sexual assault counseling
tiles.say: For sexual-assault-specialized counseling: the member centers of the Connecticut Alliance to End Sexual Violence — formerly CONNSACS — provide free counseling across the state. Call 1-888-999-5545 in English or 1-888-568-8332 in Spanish for the nearest center.

tiles.label: 988 — crisis right now
tiles.say: If you are in mental-health crisis right now — overwhelmed, suicidal thoughts, panic attacks — call or text 988. Free, confidential, twenty-four hours. The counselors are trained to support crime and DV survivors.

tiles.label: OVS pays for therapy
tiles.say: CT Office of Victim Services compensation can pay for mental-health therapy related to the crime — including with off-campus therapists you choose. Save receipts. Apply through OVS.

tiles.label: Pregnancy options
tiles.say: If you are or might be pregnant: All-Options at 1-888-493-0092 provides free, judgment-free pregnancy options counseling without pushing any specific direction. Planned Parenthood at 1-800-230-7526 also handles full options. Connecticut’s shield law — Public Act 22-19 — protects providers and people who help Connecticut residents access reproductive health care.

tiles.label: Transitional housing
tiles.say: Many CCADV member shelters operate transitional housing programs — typically up to two years — that bridge the gap between emergency shelter and permanent housing. Subsidized rent, support services, case management. Apply through your shelter or call CCADV 1-888-774-2900.

tiles.label: Permanent housing — CHFA
tiles.say: For longer-term housing assistance: CT Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) operates rental-assistance programs and first-time-homebuyer programs. The DV survivor program is specifically funded. Some CCADV shelters provide housing vouchers as part of transitional services.

tiles.label: CT Address Confidentiality Program
tiles.say: The CT Address Confidentiality Program — ACP — gives you a substitute address for public records (DMV, voter rolls, court filings, school records). Useful when you need a permanent address but cannot let the abuser know it. Apply through an enrolling agency — most CCADV shelters are agencies. CT Secretary of the State administers.

tiles.label: Job training + employment
tiles.say: CT Department of Labor and the American Job Center network offer free job training, resume help, and interview prep. CCADV member shelters also have employment specialists. Many DV survivors qualify for waivers of work requirements while stabilizing. CT 211 routes.

tiles.label: Credit + financial recovery
tiles.say: Financial abuse is part of most DV — many survivors have damaged credit, joint debt with the abuser, or were prevented from working. The Allstate Foundation Moving Ahead curriculum (free, online) teaches financial recovery. CFA — Center for Financial Action — also has free financial counseling specifically for DV survivors.

tiles.label: Immigration — VAWA / U-visa / T-visa
tiles.say: For immigration relief paths — VAWA self-petition, U-visa, T-visa for trafficking survivors, SIJS for unaccompanied minors, asylum — free legal help in Connecticut is available through IRIS in New Haven, CIRI (the Connecticut Institute for Refugees and Immigrants) in Bridgeport, and the Yale and UConn law school immigration clinics. Apply early; these can take many months to several years.

tiles.label: Name change — legal
tiles.say: In extreme cases, survivors change their legal name to add another layer of separation from the abuser. CT Probate Court handles name changes. Combined with the Address Confidentiality Program, this can be effective. Cost: filing fee (waiver available for low income). Free legal help: CT Legal Services 1-800-453-3320.

tiles.label: Long-term advocate / case manager
tiles.say: Most CCADV member shelters provide ongoing case management for months or years after the immediate crisis — court accompaniment, housing search, benefits applications, parenting support. Free. Call 1-888-774-2900 and ask about case-management services.

tiles.label: Survivors groups — peer support
tiles.say: Peer support groups — facilitated by other survivors who have been where you are — help with the long-term emotional recovery. CCADV member shelters run them; National DV Hotline can also connect you with online groups.
